title: Imports: Number Theory and Arithmetic
content: Imports Mathlib modules for divisors, prime numbers, GCD, ordered ring lemmas, and tactics. These provide the foundations for prime factorization, coprimality arguments, and ordered arithmetic on ℕ and ℚ.
mathContext: The formalization uses `Nat.primeFactors`, `Nat.gcd`, and `Nat.Prime` from Mathlib to reason about the prime structure of solutions to $x^x y^y = z^z$.

title: Solution Structure
content: Defines **Solution** as a dependent structure: a triple $(x, y, z)$ with proofs $x, y, z > 1$ and the equation $x^x \cdot y^y = z^z$. This encapsulates the constraints as a single mathematical object.
mathContext: The structure bundles the Diophantine equation $x^x y^y = z^z$ with positivity constraints $x,y,z > 1$ as a dependent record. The condition $> 1$ excludes the trivial solution $1^1 \cdot 1^1 = 1^1$.

title: Solutions Exist
content: Defines **SolutionsExist** as `Nonempty Solution` — the proposition that at least one solution exists. This is the main question of Problem #674.
mathContext: The existential statement $\exists (x,y,z), x,y,z > 1 \wedge x^x y^y = z^z$ is captured as `Nonempty Solution`, using Lean 4's `Nonempty` to express non-emptiness of the solution type.

title: Ko (1940): Solutions Exist
content: **Ko's Theorem**: YES, solutions to $x^x y^y = z^z$ exist with $x,y,z > 1$. The affirmative answer to Erdős Problem #674, proved by exhibiting an explicit example.
mathContext: Ko's 1940 paper not only established existence but initiated the systematic study of $x^x y^y = z^z$. The proof constructs a solution by choosing $x, y, z$ as products of powers of 2 and 3, then verifying the equation arithmetically.

title: Ko's Explicit Solution
content: Defines $x = 2^{12} \cdot 3^6 = 2{,}985{,}984$, $y = 2^8 \cdot 3^8 = 1{,}679{,}616$, $z = 2^{11} \cdot 3^7 = 4{,}478{,}976$. This is Ko's smallest known explicit solution to $x^x y^y = z^z$.
mathContext: Ko's example uses only primes 2 and 3. Taking logarithms: $x \log x + y \log y = z \log z$, which requires $(12 \log 2 + 6 \log 3)(12 \log 2 + 6 \log 3) + (8 \log 2 + 8 \log 3)(8 \log 2 + 8 \log 3) = (11 \log 2 + 7 \log 3)(11 \log 2 + 7 \log 3)$ to balance.

title: Ko's Solution Validity
content: States that Ko's example satisfies $\text{koX}^{\text{koX}} \cdot \text{koY}^{\text{koY}} = \text{koZ}^{\text{koZ}}$. This is a computational verification requiring enormous arithmetic (numbers with millions of digits).
mathContext: Verifying $x^x y^y = z^z$ for $x \approx 3 \times 10^6$ requires computing numbers with $\sim 10^7$ digits. The sorry reflects the impracticality of `norm_num` for such large computations; a certificate-based approach or modular verification would be needed.

title: No Coprime Solutions (Ko 1940)
content: **No coprime solutions**: If $\gcd(x,y) = 1$ then $x^x y^y = z^z$ has no solution with $x,y,z > 1$. This means every solution must have shared prime factors between $x$ and $y$.
mathContext: If $\gcd(x,y) = 1$ and $p \mid x$, then $v_p(x^x y^y) = x \cdot v_p(x)$ (since $p \nmid y$). For $z^z$, $v_p(z^z) = z \cdot v_p(z)$. The equation forces $x \cdot v_p(x) = z \cdot v_p(z)$, but careful analysis shows this leads to a contradiction when $\gcd(x,y) = 1$.

title: Schinzel (1958): Shared Prime Divisors
content: **Schinzel's Theorem**: For any solution and any prime $p$, $p \mid x \iff p \mid y$. This strengthens Ko's coprimality result: not just $\gcd(x,y) > 1$, but $x$ and $y$ have exactly the same prime divisors.
mathContext: Schinzel proved that if $p \mid x$ but $p \nmid y$, then $v_p(x^x y^y) = x \cdot v_p(x)$ while $v_p(z^z) = z \cdot v_p(z)$, forcing $z \cdot v_p(z) = x \cdot v_p(x)$. Combined with the equation $x + y = z + \text{(correction)}$ from the logarithmic form, this yields a contradiction.

title: Schinzel's Conjecture (Full Version)
content: Defines **SchinzelConjecture**: for all solutions, $p \mid x \iff p \mid y$ AND $p \mid y \iff p \mid z$. This extends Schinzel's 1958 result to include $z$, conjecturing all three variables share identical prime factors.
mathContext: The full conjecture states $\text{rad}(x) = \text{rad}(y) = \text{rad}(z)$, where $\text{rad}(n) = \prod_{p \mid n} p$ is the radical. Dem'janenko (1975) proved this conjecture.

title: Dem'janenko (1975): Identical Prime Factors
content: **Dem'janenko's Theorem**: Schinzel's conjecture is true — all three variables $x, y, z$ share identical prime factors. This is the deepest structural result about solutions to $x^x y^y = z^z$.
mathContext: Dem'janenko's proof analyzes the equation $x \log x + y \log y = z \log z$ using properties of the strictly convex function $t \mapsto t \log t$. Combined with $p$-adic valuation arguments, this forces $\text{primeFactors}(x) = \text{primeFactors}(y) = \text{primeFactors}(z)$.

title: Ratio Q = xy/z²
content: Defines **ratioQ(s)** = xy/z² as a rational number. This parameter classifies solutions: Ko's family achieves Q = 1/4 (equality in 4xy = z²), and Mills proved Q ≤ 1/4 universally.
mathContext: The ratio $Q = xy/z^2$ is the key invariant for solution classification. By AM-GM applied to the logarithmic equation, $Q \le 1/4$ with equality iff the exponents in the prime factorization satisfy a specific balance condition.

title: Mills' Constraint: No Solutions with 4xy > z²
content: **Mills' Theorem**: No non-trivial solutions satisfy $4xy > z^2$ (i.e., $Q > 1/4$) when $x \ne y$. This restricts all solutions to the region $Q \le 1/4$.
mathContext: Mills proved this using the concavity of $\log$: from $x \log x + y \log y = z \log z$ and $x + y > z$ (which holds when $4xy > z^2$), one derives a contradiction via Jensen's inequality for $t \mapsto t \log t$.

title: Ko's Family: 4xy = z²
content: Ko's explicit example satisfies $4 \cdot \text{koX} \cdot \text{koY} = \text{koZ}^2$, i.e., $Q = 1/4$. This can be verified: $4 \cdot 2^{12} \cdot 3^6 \cdot 2^8 \cdot 3^8 = 2^{22} \cdot 3^{14} = (2^{11} \cdot 3^7)^2$.
mathContext: The identity $4xy = z^2$ for Ko's example follows from $4 \cdot 2^{20} \cdot 3^{14} = 2^{22} \cdot 3^{14} = (2^{11} \cdot 3^7)^2$. This equality characterizes Ko's family among all solutions.

title: Uchiyama (1984): Finiteness for Fixed Q
content: **Uchiyama's Theorem**: For each fixed $Q \in (0, 1/4)$, the set of solutions with $\text{ratioQ}(s) = Q$ is finite. Uses Baker's theory of linear forms in logarithms.
mathContext: Baker's theorem gives effective lower bounds for $|\alpha_1^{b_1} \cdots \alpha_m^{b_m} - 1|$ where $\alpha_i$ are algebraic and $b_i$ integers. Applied to $x^x y^y / z^z = 1$, this bounds the $p$-adic valuations and hence the size of solutions for fixed $Q$.

title: Ko's Parametric Family
content: Defines **koFamily(n)** for $n \ge 2$: set $a = 2^{n+1}$, $b = 2^n - 1$, base $= 2^{a(b-n)} \cdot b^{2b}$, then $(x,y,z) = (\text{base} \cdot 2^{2n}, \text{base} \cdot b^2, \text{base} \cdot 2^{n+1} \cdot b)$.
mathContext: Ko's construction uses $a = 2^{n+1}$ and $b = 2^n - 1$ (a Mersenne-like number). The key identity is $a = 2b + 2 - 2^{-(n-1)}\cdot(\ldots)$, which ensures $x^x y^y = z^z$ balances. For $n = 2$: $a = 8$, $b = 3$, recovering the example $x = 2^{12} \cdot 3^6$.

title: Infinitely Many Solutions
content: Ko's parametric family produces infinitely many distinct solutions to $x^x y^y = z^z$. Since different $n \ge 2$ yield different solutions (the prime factorization changes), the solution set is infinite.
mathContext: The proof shows `koFamily` is injective for $n \ge 2$ (different $n$ give different $b = 2^n - 1$, hence different prime factorizations). Combined with `ko_family_valid`, this gives $|\{s : \text{Solution} \mid \top\}| = \infty$.

title: Ko Type Solutions
content: A solution is **Ko type** if it equals `koFamily(n)` for some $n \ge 2$. The open question is whether ALL solutions are of Ko type (i.e., whether Ko's family is exhaustive).
mathContext: The conjecture $\text{KoConjectureFull}: \forall s, \text{IsKoType}(s)$ would mean the solution set of $x^x y^y = z^z$ is exactly $\{\text{koFamily}(n) \mid n \ge 2\}$. Mills' computational evidence supports this but no proof exists.

title: Universal Ratio Constraint Q ≤ 1/4
content: Every solution satisfies $Q = xy/z^2 \le 1/4$, i.e., $4xy \le z^2$. This universal bound partitions the problem: equality ($Q = 1/4$) is Ko's family, and strict inequality ($Q < 1/4$) has only finitely many solutions per fixed $Q$.
mathContext: The bound $Q \le 1/4$ follows from AM-GM: $xy \le ((x+y)/2)^2$ combined with $z \le x + y - 1$ (from the logarithmic equation). Equality holds iff the prime factorization exponents satisfy a specific balance.

title: Small Cases: No Solutions for x = 2, 3, or x = y
content: No solutions with $x = 2$ (since $4 y^y = z^z$ forces contradictory 2-adic valuations), $x = 3$ (similar argument with 3-adic valuations), or $x = y$ (since $x^{2x} = z^z$ requires $z = x^{2x/z}$ which has no integer solutions for $x,z > 1$).
mathContext: For $x = 2$: $4 y^y = z^z$ gives $v_2(z^z) = v_2(4 y^y) = 2 + y \cdot v_2(y)$. Since $z \cdot v_2(z) = 2 + y \cdot v_2(y)$, careful case analysis on the parity of $y$ yields contradictions. The $x = y$ case reduces to $x^{2x} = z^z$.

title: Ordering: x < z < y
content: In any solution with $x \le y$, the ordering is $x < z < y$. This follows from the strict convexity of $t \mapsto t \log t$: the equation $x \log x + y \log y = z \log z$ forces $z$ to lie strictly between $x$ and $y$.
mathContext: Since $f(t) = t \log t$ is strictly convex for $t > 0$, the equation $f(x) + f(y) = f(z)$ with $x < y$ implies $f(x) < f(z) < f(x) + f(y)$, and by monotonicity of $f$, $x < z < y$ (for $x,y,z$ large enough).
